Across twenty tests, the chance that at least one fires is sixty-four percent. Peeking at a running experiment, and stopping when p dips under point zero five, does the same thing, one look at a time. The cure is deciding before you look: the question, the sample and the analysis, all fixed in advance. Or raise the bar for every test. Twenty tests sharing five percent means each one needs point zero zero two five. But even a test played fairly can be wrong, in two ways.

Cross what's true with what you decide, and you get four outcomes. Reject a null that's true, and that's a false alarm, a Type One error. Its rate is alpha. Miss an effect that's real, and that's a Type Two error, with rate beta. The cell beside it is power: the chance of catching an effect that's really there.

Power is easiest to see by counting. Plant a real effect of half a standard deviation, test thirty per group, and repeat two thousand times. Forty-seven and a half percent of the runs reject. Finding an effect that's really there is a coin flip. Lower alpha to cut false alarms, and you miss even more. With the sample fixed, pushing one error down pushes the other up. Only more data shrinks both. Forty per group catches this effect sixty-one percent of the time. Eighty catches ninety. Studies are usually designed for at least eighty percent.

That's why an A-B test is sized before it starts. To catch a lift from ten percent to twelve, with eighty percent power, takes three thousand, eight hundred and forty-one users in each arm. Halve the lift, to eleven, and it takes fourteen thousand, seven hundred and fifty-one. Nearly four times as many.
